Distance multiplier during manual pulling (onPull).

• Value >= 1.0: Linear following of the finger.
• Value < 1.0: Enables non-linear resistance (rubber band effect) — the further you pull, the stronger the resistance.
Spring stiffness constant (k).\n\nDetermines the force returning the list to its original position. Affects the oscillation frequency during bounce.
Damping ratio (ζ).\n\nDissipates spring energy. Determines how quickly oscillations settle after releasing the finger or hitting a boundary.

Incoming velocity multiplier during onAbsorb (inertial impact).

Increases bounce amplitude during rapid scrolling.
Note: At high values (>1.0), the code dynamically reduces spring stiffness to make the impact feel "softer".
Exponent power for the resistance formula.\n\nWorks only if Pull Coefficient < 1.0. Defines the steepness of force increase when pulling the edge.

Changes ScaleY of the RenderNode content vertically.

• Shrink: flattens content on impact.
• Grow: elongates content (rubber effect).
Changes the overall scale (ScaleX and ScaleY) of the entire container.\n\nCreates a zoom in/out effect when interacting with the boundary.
Changes ScaleX along the width.\n\nAllows for a "barrel" or narrowing effect when stretching.
Coefficient of displacement influence on scale. Higher values mean stronger distortion for the same displacement.
Hard distortion limit (min/max scale) to prevent visual artifacts during strong pulls.
Pivot coordinate for scaling (0.0 - 1.0). 0.5 is center.
Spring cutoff velocity threshold.\n\nDetermines when physics calculations are forcibly stopped. If spring velocity falls below this value, animation ends. Helps remove micro-jitter at the end.

Amplitude cutoff threshold.\n\nIf residual displacement (in pixels) becomes less than this value, animation is considered complete. Increasing this makes the return to zero visually sharper and faster.

Automatically mirrors anchor coordinates when interacting with the right or bottom edge.

• ON: Coordinate 0.0 always means "the edge being pulled".
• OFF: Coordinates are absolute (0.0 is always left/top, 1.0 is always right/bottom), regardless of swipe direction.
Scaling point along the main axis (scroll direction) for horizontal lists.\n\nDetermines which part of the screen width is primarily distorted during pull.
Scaling point along the cross axis (height) for horizontal lists.\n\nAllows shifting the center of the effect up or down relative to the list center.
Determines effect strength exclusively for horizontal lists (LazyRow, ViewPager). Allows tuning behavior separately from vertical scrolling.
Low-pass filter for finger coordinates in onPull.\n\nSmoothes sensor noise before passing data to the physics model. High values make the reaction feel "viscous".

Global animation speed multiplier.

Applied on top of all physics and visual settings.
100%% = default speed, below 100%% slows down, above 100%% speeds up.
Interpolation speed (LERP) during direct interaction (onPull).\n\nDetermines how fast the visual catches up to the finger while the spring is NOT running (disabled). Lower = smoother, but with lag.
Interpolation speed (LERP) during active animation (onRelease/onAbsorb).\n\nDetermines movement smoothness when the physics model is running (spring active).

Normalization coefficient for Jetpack Compose.\n\nCompose passes scroll deltas in different units or aggregates them differently. This divider reduces incoming onPull values to align physics with the View system.

Unlike Qualcomm chips, heat management in Google Tensor is handled via configuration files (thermal_info_config.json) rather than direct kernel parameters.

This module works at the system level: it changes a specific property (prop) that forces the Thermal HAL service to load an alternative configuration file with different throttling thresholds.

This is a safe, "native" adjustment method provided by Pixel architecture. A reboot is required to apply changes.
Standard factory limits. Ensures maximum safety and battery lifespan.
Slight threshold increase (+5°C). Helps avoid charging slowdowns during moderate heating.
Balanced profile (+9°C). Compromise between charging speed and body heat.
WARNING: High limits (+15°C). Noticeable heating possible during fast charging. Accelerates battery chemistry wear.
DANGER: Almost complete disablement of thermal protection (+90°C). High risk of battery swelling and device damage.
Standard algorithm. Aggressive frequency reduction (throttling) to keep the body temperature low.
Soft profile (+5°C). Allows the processor to maintain high frequencies longer under load.
Optimal for gaming (+9°C). Significantly reduces FPS drops; device will be warm.
Maximum performance (+15°C). Device may become hot to the touch. Recommended only for short-term tasks.
EXTREME: Throttling disabled. Processor will heat up until emergency power shutdown. Benchmarks only.
New thermal profile selected.\n\nThe Thermal HAL service will read new settings only on the next system boot. Reboot device now?

WARNING: You selected an aggressive thermal mode!

This may lead to severe overheating and accelerated component degradation.

A reboot is required to apply settings.

These settings forcibly activate Carrier Config capabilities. By default, most of these features are hidden or disabled for uncertified regions.\n\nAirplane Mode toggle is required to apply changes.
These settings forcibly activate Carrier Config capabilities. By default, most of these features are hidden or disabled for uncertified regions.\n\nAirplane Mode toggle is required to apply changes.

Forcibly enables VoLTE support in carrier configuration.\n\nAllows making voice calls over 4G/LTE network without switching to 3G/2G. Ensures fast connection, HD sound quality, and simultaneous internet usage during calls. Fixes missing VoLTE toggle in settings.

Forcibly enables Wi-Fi Calling support.\n\nAllows phone to register in carrier IMS network via any available Wi-Fi. Indispensable in places with poor cellular reception (basements, thick walls) but internet access. Activates hidden "Wi-Fi Calling" menu.
Enables native video calling support via carrier.\n\nThis is built-in dialer video function (not via messengers, but standard IR.94 protocol). Works if carrier supports Video over LTE.

Backup calling technology via another SIM.\n\nAllows using internet traffic of the second SIM to register IMS services for the first SIM. Useful when the main SIM lost network (e.g., roaming or dead zone) but the second SIM has internet access.

Voice over New Radio. Voice calls in pure 5G networks (Standalone).\n\nThe most modern voice transmission standard. Ensures ultra-low latency and better quality than VoLTE. Works only in 5G SA networks and requires Android 14+.

Removes software 5G block from configuration side.\n\nMany carriers block 5G access for Pixel devices not in their "whitelist", even if hardware support exists. This switch forcibly adds NR NSA and SA bands to the allowed list.

Modifies signal level thresholds (RSRP) for network switching.\n\nLowers signal quality requirements for showing 5G icon and staying in 5G network. Helps if phone drops to 4G/LTE too eagerly even when 5G is available.

Supplementary service management via IMS.\n\nAllows configuring call forwarding, call waiting, and caller ID via phone settings menu using IP channel instead of obsolete USSD codes. Fixes "Network or SIM card error" when trying to access call settings in LTE-only networks.

Root JSON value must be an object
PID controller parameter. It changes how quickly and strongly a cooling device reduces power during overheating.
Sensor to cooling-device binding. These fields tell Thermal HAL which limit to apply when thresholds are reached.
Thermal HAL profile override. BindedCdevInfo size and contents must stay compatible with the base sensor list.
Thermal HAL statistics field. It affects thermal metrics logging and usually does not change throttling itself.
Unknown PixelParts JSON field. It will be saved as-is into the final config. Check thermal_info.cpp or the stock vendor config before editing.
AIDL thermal entity type: BATTERY, SKIN, CPU, GPU, USB_PORT, and others. Framework uses it for callbacks, UI, and system decisions.
Seven hot thresholds by thermal severity: NONE, LIGHT, MODERATE, SEVERE, CRITICAL, EMERGENCY, SHUTDOWN. Higher values delay that throttling level. "NaN" disables a level.
Hysteresis for leaving a hot severity level. Thermal HAL clears severity only after temperature drops below HotThreshold minus this value.
Cold severity thresholds. They are less common than hot thresholds, but use the same seven-level array. "NaN" disables a level.
Hysteresis for cold severity. It avoids rapid state changes when the sensor value is near a boundary.
Raw sensor or sysfs multiplier. On many Pixel thermal nodes, 0.001 converts millidegrees to Celsius.
Active sensor polling interval in milliseconds when the sensor is not in the passive throttling loop. Lower values react faster but add wakeups.
Polling interval in passive or active throttling mode. It strongly affects PID and hard-limit throttling response.
Virtual sensor flag. The value is calculated from other sensors instead of being read directly from sysfs or a property.
Virtual sensor or virtual rail formula, such as MAXIMUM or WEIGHTED_AVG, plus other parser-supported variants.
Input sensors or power rails for a virtual value. Order must match Coefficient.
Weights for Combination. In weighted-average cases, they define each input contribution to final temperature or power.
Coefficient type for the formula. The parser uses it to interpret the Coefficient array correctly.
Input entity type for virtual calculation. It distinguishes sensor and rail combinations in extended configs.
Offset applied after virtual sensor formula calculation. Often used by Pixel skin temperature calibration models.
Sensors whose events wake the virtual sensor and recalculate its value.
Allows framework callbacks when sensor severity changes. It affects Android ThermalService and apps listening to thermal status.
Allows Thermal HAL to send a PowerHAL hint when sensor state changes. It can change scheduler and performance behavior.
Hides the sensor from public lists without disabling its internal use by virtual sensors or throttling rules.
Model or schema version for a specific sensor. Usually informational for the Pixel thermal model.
Runtime overrides for thermal modes. They usually change BindedCdevInfo limits, while the cooling-device list must stay compatible with the base config.
Thermal profile mode name for the override. HAL applies it through its profile mechanism when the system selects that mode.
PID controller block. It calculates requested power for cooling devices from the error between current temperature and threshold.
PID proportional coefficient while overheating above the threshold. Higher values cut power faster and harder.
PID proportional coefficient while returning below the threshold. It affects power recovery after cooling.
PID integral coefficient. It accumulates error over time; too high can hold throttling too long or make the system oscillate.
Integral coefficient for the overshoot path when the config separates K_I for overheating and recovery.
Integral coefficient for the undershoot or recovery path when the config separates K_I.
PID differential coefficient. It reacts to temperature change speed and usually helps smooth sudden spikes.
Upper limit for the PID integral term. It prevents endless accumulation of throttling request.
Sustainable power for the PID model. HAL uses it as the base power around which it calculates the power budget.
Minimum power that PID can allocate to the bound cooling device.
Maximum power that PID can allocate to the bound cooling device. It usually caps performance during heating.
Cutoff threshold for the PID integral term. It helps avoid integral accumulation when error is small or the mode is stable.
Initial PID integral value. Used as the controller starting point.
Initial PID integral value as a percentage of the allowed range.
Integral or recovery trend. Extra parser setting for PID behavior while temperature changes.
PID transition cycle. It affects how quickly the controller moves between states.
Cooling devices bound to the sensor. This turns sensor severity or PID request into real frequency or power limits.
Cooling device name from the CoolingDevices section. It must match exactly or Thermal HAL cannot apply the limit.
Hard-limit values for seven severity levels. Usually a cooling state: 0 means no limit, higher values mean stronger limits.
Alternative hard-limit expressed as frequencies when the cooling device uses frequency mapping.
Cooling-state ceiling for PID by severity. It limits how far PID can throttle the device.
Frequency ceiling for the PID or frequency cooling path.
Weight of a cooling device in PID allocation. It distributes thermal budget between CPU, GPU, TPU, and other cooling devices.
Maximum limit release step per cycle. Lower values make recovery smoother.
Maximum throttle increase step per cycle. Higher values cut performance faster during overheating.
Power rail bound to a cooling device for power accounting. It must match the PowerRails section.
Power threshold for power-based throttling logic or exceptions when configured.
Hard-limit release rule. It changes the conditions under which HAL restores performance.
Disables a specific cooling-device binding in a profile override without removing it from the schema.
Sysfs path where Thermal HAL writes cooling state or limit. A wrong path makes the cooling device ineffective.
Cooling state to power table. PID and power allocation use it to convert state to power budget.
Power rail name that provides energy or power statistics for a cooling device or sensor.
Delay between power samples in milliseconds. It affects power rail measurement accuracy and latency.
Number of samples used to average power rail data. More samples are steadier but react slower.
Virtual power rail flag. The value is built from Combination and Coefficient instead of being read directly.
Entities for which stats helper records events using default thresholds.
Entities with custom thresholds for thermal stats. They do not have to match throttling thresholds.
Enables default threshold logging for every entity in the stats section.
Statistic threshold values. They must be sorted ascending or the parser rejects the stats block.
Metric name written by stats helper. Useful when one physical value is logged in multiple ways.
Abnormal thermal behavior detection settings, such as outlier and stuck sensor diagnostics.
Temperature outlier detection config relative to the allowed range.
Stuck sensor detection config for a sensor value that does not change for too long.
Sensors or cooling devices monitored by stats or abnormality logic.
Allowed temperature range for outlier detection.
Stuck-sensor detection parameters: how many polls and how long the value may remain unchanged.
Minimum number of polling cycles before stuck detection can consider a problem valid.
Minimum unchanged-temperature duration for stuck detection.
Cooling-device vote statistics per sensor. Helps identify which sensor requested throttling.
Power accounting exclusions for a sensor. Used when part of a rail or cooling device must be excluded from calculations.
Prediction model block for a sensor. The parser uses it to forecast temperature over a future horizon.
Prediction model weights. Wrong count or scale can make the forecast useless.
Additional JSON configs. PixelParts HAL supports absolute paths starting with slash and relative names from /vendor/etc.

Intelligent normalization system for Jetpack Compose scroll implementations.

Compose passes amplified deltas compared to classic View scrolls. This module automatically detects Compose instances and smoothly reduces their deltas to match standard View behavior.

Calibrated from empirical data: Compose deltas are ~5× larger than View deltas for identical gestures.

Master switch for intelligent delta normalization.

When enabled, the system analyzes each EdgeEffect instance and applies correction factor to Compose-amplified deltas.

Safe to leave on — does nothing for apps with normal deltas.

Baseline "normal" delta value (fraction of effectiveSize).

Determined empirically from View-based apps. If the running mean exceeds this × Detect Multiplier, the instance is considered amplified.

Default: 0.00001 (very sensitive). Increase if false positives occur on normal apps.

Threshold multiplier for amplification detection.

Activation: running_mean > ref_delta × this.
3.3 = reliably catches Compose (~5× from View), won't trigger on View apps.

Increase if false positives, decrease if not catching Compose.

How much to multiply amplified deltas by.

0.2 = bring to View level (from analysis: ref/compose ≈ 0.195).
0.5 = halve the delta. 1.0 = no change.

Smaller = weaker bounce, larger = stronger.

Number of recent |delta| samples to analyze.

Smaller = faster detection (reacts in fewer events) but more noise-sensitive.
 Larger = more stable but slower to adapt.

Range: 2–64.

How many events to transition from 1.0 to factor.

1–4 = near-instant. 8–12 = smooth transition.

Prevents visual jumps when normalization activates.

How Compose instances are identified.

0 = Behavior only (sliding window of deltas)
1 = Hybrid: stack trace gives instant ID, window confirms
2 = Stack trace only (no window analysis)

Hybrid (1) is recommended for best accuracy + speed.
